newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan police clash with slain Bhutto supporters.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan police clash with slain Bhutto supporters.

text.p: Pakistani police fired bullets and teargas on Monday to disperse supporters of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's dead brother Murtaza in Larkana, witnesses said.

Two of the supporters were wounded, witnesses said. Leaders of Murtaza's breakaway faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP), known as PPP-Shaheed Bhutto, said one person had been killed, but this could not be confirmed.
Murtaza, 42, was killed in a gunbattle between his bodyguards and police in Karachi on Friday night.
Benazir and her mother Nusrat Bhutto planned to leave Larkana later on Monday to receive condolences in Karachi.
Murtaza's Lebanese widow Ghinwa was expected to fly separately to the southern port city.
The PPP-Shaheed Bhutto faction invited Ghinwa to become its leader, but party sources said she was unlikely to declare her intentions until a 40-day Moslem mourning period was over.

Murtaza's party issued a statement on Monday accusing police of shooting their leader and 11 of his followers in an ambush and delaying the transfer of the dead and wounded to a hospital, which was inadequately equipped to cope with the casualties.
"The assassination of Murtaza Bhutto and his six companions was no accident but was a brutal and deliberate act of state terrorism," the statement said.
Police say they fired in self-defence after Murtaza's bodyguards began shooting to prevent police checks.
Opposition politicians and newspapers have criticised police in Karachi for being trigger-happy and undisciplined.

"The real culprits should be arrested and punished," Rao Rashid, secretary-general of PPP-Shaheed Bhutto, told a news conference in Larkana. He urged Pakistanis to take part in a day of anti-government strikes, protests and marches on Thursday.
The party also demanded that a Supreme Court judge investigate Murtaza's killing rather than the provincial high court judge already named by the Sindh province government.

Murtaza's death has shaken Benazir Bhutto, who inherited the PPP leadership mantle from her father, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was ousted as prime minister in a 1977 coup and executed in 1979 by former military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq.

Murtaza challenged her leadership when he returned in 1993 after 16 years in self-imposed exile, mainly in Syria. He set up his rival group in March last year, but attracted no political heavyweights from his sister's mainstream party.
But political sources said protests in Murtaza's home province of Sindh and some other parts of Pakistan after his death showed that Murtaza had built up considerable support.

If she accepts the leadership offer, Ghinwa, a former teacher who speaks English and French as well as her native Arabic, would become the first Arab woman to lead a Pakistani political group, although not the first foreign-born.
Her Iranian-born mother-in-law Nusrat became figurehead PPP chief after Zulfikar Bhutto's execution. Benazir had her removed as leader in 1993, but her Iranian roots were not an issue.
